title: The Mason's Son: Buschiazzo, the Recoleta Gate, and the Cutting of Colonial Buenos Aires
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pontinvrea: the mason's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and town confirmed by es.wikipedia. The region is corrected here: Pontinvrea is in Liguria, province of Savona, not Piedmont, though both lay inside the Kingdom of Sardinia. Coordinates taken from it.wikipedia, discarding two other values in circulation that miss the town by 3 to 5 km
stops.campa: In a stone village in the hills above Savona, inside the Kingdom of Sardinia, a son is entered in the parish register as Giovanni Antonio Buschiazzo. His father is a master mason, in the trade of a region whose men leave home each season to raise walls somewhere else and come back for the winter. This family will not come back. Within five years they cross an ocean instead of a valley, and the boy who cannot yet write his name will spend his life building a capital on the other side of it. Pontinvrea's own histories do not mention him.
suggested_refs: The parish register of Pontinvrea, province of Savona, for October 1845 (not consulted; named as a gap)

stops.name: The Bajo of Buenos Aires: the family comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. es.wikipedia says only that he arrived at four years old and gives no year; en.wikipedia gives 1850; born October 1845, age four spans October 1849 to October 1850. The landing point is the pre-mole Bajo below the Plaza de Mayo, not the Darsena Sur dug decades later. No passenger manifest for this crossing has been found
stops.campa: The port has no docks. Ships anchor offshore in the open roadstead and passengers are rowed in and then carted through the mud below the Plaza de Mayo, with the luggage held above the water. Juan Antonio is four, or nearly five, one of a wave of Ligurian and Piedmontese families arriving to remake the edges of the city. What is certain is where the family goes next. Not to the waterfront, but inland to a separate village of orchards north of the town, where masons are wanted and land is cheap.
suggested_refs: Passenger lists for the port of Buenos Aires, c.1850 (none located)

stops.name: Belgrano: the trade watched and then learned
stops.date_confidence: the family's settlement in Belgrano is attested; the specific year is a placeholder inside the 1850s, which is all the sources support
stops.campa: Belgrano is its own town, low houses and orchards and mud streets, not yet part of Buenos Aires and not expecting to be. The father works the trade he brought from Liguria. Four more children are born here, all Argentine by birth where the eldest is not, and the eldest learns the trade the way it has always been learned, by carrying things for men who are building. He is thirty-three before any institution certifies what he knows. The first public building he designs will stand a few blocks from this house.
suggested_refs: The pueblo of Belgrano before its 1888 annexation to the federal capital

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the studio of Nicolas Canale
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; the studio's address does not survive in any source consulted, and the coordinate is the historic centre as a placeholder
stops.campa: At seventeen he enters the studio of the Italian architect Nicolas Canale and his son Jose, and moves from the scaffold to the drafting table. Buenos Aires has no school of architecture; the profession is passed hand to hand, master to apprentice, plan to built wall, and this is the only training available in the country. He spends years here. The studio's address has not survived in anything reachable, only the fact that he was in it, which is how most apprenticeships of the period survive.
suggested_refs: Nicolas Canale and Jose Canale, Italian architects working in Buenos Aires from the 1850s

stops.name: Belgrano: the Casa Municipal on Cuba street
stops.date_confidence: the building's own article dates the design to 1873; the biography and earlier working notes give 1874. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus pin already used for this building, which sits about 250 m from the coordinate printed in the museum's own article
stops.campa: He builds a petit hotel on Cuba street for the council of a town with fifteen years of independence left: six Roman Doric columns over a shallow flight of steps, Italian Renaissance in its bones and Mannerist in its ornament. He has no diploma yet. In 1880, when Buenos Aires is federalized and the national government needs a roof while the question is settled, this building holds the executive, the legislature and the courts at once. It serves Belgrano as its municipal seat until 1888 and becomes a museum in 1938.
suggested_refs: The Museo Historico Sarmiento, Cuba 2079, formerly the Casa Municipal de Belgrano

stops.name: Saavedra: streets drawn on open ground
stops.date_confidence: no date in any source consulted. Placed before the 1880 municipal appointment, which is the only chronological constraint the record gives; the year is a placeholder
stops.campa: North of Belgrano, on ground that is still mostly open, he lays out the streets of Saavedra: no gate, no portico, no columns, just a grid drawn for a district that does not exist yet and a decision about where people will one day walk. The work appears in the catalogue of his early commissions without a date, without a named client, and without any account of what he actually decided or how much of it was built. It is the first time he is handed a piece of the map rather than a building on it.
suggested_refs: The street plan of Saavedra, northern edge of the federal capital

stops.name: Belgrano: a seat on the Comision de Obras Publicas
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia; no month given
stops.campa: He takes a seat on Belgrano's Municipal Commission of Public Works: drainage, paving, the small unglamorous infrastructure of a town that still believes it will stay a town. It is his first standing as a public official rather than a private draftsman. Within five years the place will be absorbed into the capital, the commission will be dissolved into a metropolitan department, and he will be running that department. He is thirty. He still has no diploma of any kind.
suggested_refs: The Comision Municipal de Obras Publicas de Belgrano, 1875

stops.name: Facultad de Ciencias Fisico-Matematicas: the disputed diploma
stops.date_confidence: unresolved contradiction. es.wikipedia: graduates 1878 from the faculty founded in 1874, the second diploma it ever issues. en.wikipedia: graduates 1869 in architecture and construction engineering, qualifying formally as architect only in 1878. Both cannot be first; nothing reachable adjudicates, and the two accounts are left standing
stops.campa: The Faculty of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, four years old, is the first institution in the country able to certify an architect. He enrols as a working draftsman already past thirty and takes a diploma, by the Spanish account the second the faculty ever issues. The English account has him graduating nine years earlier and only qualifying formally now. Both cannot be first. He has already built a town hall and platted a neighbourhood; the paper is the last thing to arrive.
suggested_refs: Facultad de Ciencias Fisico-Matematicas, Universidad de Buenos Aires, founded 1874

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the Departamento de Obras Publicas
stops.date_confidence: the 1880 appointment is attested by both encyclopedias. The title commonly attached to Alvear in this year is wrong: es.wikipedia gives his intendencia as 10 May 1883 to 10 May 1887, and in 1880 he headed the Comision Municipal
stops.campa: Buenos Aires becomes the federal capital and gets a public works department to match its new standing. Torcuato de Alvear, at the head of the municipal commission and from 1883 the city's first intendente, puts Buschiazzo in charge of it. The city they inherit is still largely colonial: narrow streets, a plaza cut in two by an arcade, a Cabildo with its old proportions intact. For the next decade almost everything demolished in the centre is demolished on this desk's authority, and almost every new line through it is his.
suggested_refs: The federalization of Buenos Aires, 1880, and the founding of the municipal Departamento de Obras Publicas

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: Buschiazzo is called in
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and the coordinate are both inherited unchanged from the corresponding stop in the Alvear file, where the commission is recorded from the other side
stops.campa: Alvear hands him the Recoleta: the field behind the Franciscan convent where the city has buried its dead since 1822, ungated, unpaved, grown crooked by accretion. The order is to make a necropolis of it, laid out the way a city is laid out, with streets that go somewhere and a front door that means something. Buschiazzo is thirty-five and two years past his diploma. Nobody writes down, because nobody has reason to, that he is surveying the ground he will be carried into thirty-seven years from now.
suggested_refs: Torcuato de Alvear's commission to the municipal architect, December 1880

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the wall, the streets, the portico
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by es.wikipedia; no month recorded
stops.campa: A brick wall goes round the field. The internal streets are paved and given lines, so that the tombs stand along avenues instead of wherever a family happened to buy. At the front he sets four Doric columns under a plain entablature and cuts two sentences into the stone, one for the dead and one for what the dead are waiting for. Behind that gate the richest families in Argentina will spend the next eighty years outbuilding one another in marble. The gate does not compete with them.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the entrance portal of the Cementerio de la Recoleta, paired with Expectamus Dominum, per es.wikipedia, Cementerio de la Recoleta
suggested_refs: The neoclassical portico of the Cementerio de la Recoleta, 1881

stops.name: Asilo de Mendigos: the pavilion and the chapel
stops.date_confidence: the work is a span, not a point: 1881-1885 for the pavilion and chapel, with further interventions in 1893-94 and 1897. Earlier notes called this commission undated, which was wrong, and called the institution an asylum for the elderly, which is its 1944 name, not its 1858 one
stops.campa: A few steps up the slope from his gate stands the Asilo de Mendigos, the asylum for beggars opened on this ground in 1858 under governor Valentin Alsina. As municipal architect he builds its access pavilion in an Italianate manner and its chapel in neo-Gothic, and comes back twice in the nineties to add to what he has added. The institution is renamed for the elderly in 1944 and becomes galleries later still. Two of his Recoleta commissions stand within sight of each other: one for the destitute living, one for the wealthy dead.
suggested_refs: The Italianate pavilion and neo-Gothic chapel of the Asilo de Mendigos, today the Centro Cultural Recoleta

stops.name: La Plata: the commission on empty pampa
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia; no month given, and the coordinate is Plaza Moreno at the plan's centre rather than any building of his
stops.campa: The province, stripped of its capital, decides to build another from nothing on open pampa, and Buschiazzo joins the commission overseeing the works. The plan is a grid crossed by diagonals meeting at parks and plazas at fixed intervals, drawn before a single building exists, on ground where nothing has to be removed to make room for it. He will spend the rest of his career doing the reverse: forcing straight lines through a city already built, where every metre of new street is bought with a demolition.
suggested_refs: The 1882 foundational plan of La Plata, grid and diagonals

stops.name: La Plata: the bank, and a memoir on tenement housing
stops.date_confidence: the Banco de la Provincia building and its branches carry no date in any source consulted. The year given here is the publication year of the Anales volume holding his tenement memoir, which is the only dated document tying him to La Plata construction
stops.campa: He designs the Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires here, and branches for it elsewhere in the province, in a city determined to prove it can function and not merely be planned. He also writes up, for the scientific society, a project for a great tenement house commissioned by the Banco Constructor: how to house working families at a price a bank will accept. The bank buildings carry no dates in the record. What survives dated is the paper, and of the paper only its heading can now be read.
stops.quote: Memoria descriptiva del proyecto para la construccion de una gran casa de inquilinato para el Banco Constructor de la Plata, por Juan A. Buschiazzo
stops.quote_source: Table of contents, Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 21 (1886), es.wikisource; the article body was not retrievable
suggested_refs: Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 21, p. 134

stops.name: Hospital San Roque: the municipal architect's hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested. The hospital's own article names him directly as the designer and gives the inauguration date, which corrects two earlier errors: that the commission was undated, and a coordinate 1.3 km east of the real site
stops.campa: The site has been in provisional hospital use since the cholera of 1868, sheds and tents on the edge of the built city. The municipal architect designs the permanent complex, and in August it is inaugurated as the Hospital San Roque. It is the first in a series that will run thirty years and put his hand on much of the capital's public hospital system, most of it recorded in lists rather than in drawings. The hospital is renamed for Ramos Mejia and is working still.
suggested_refs: Hospital General de Agudos Dr. Jose Maria Ramos Mejia, inaugurated as Hospital San Roque, 12 August 1883

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the central arch of the Recova
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia, Recova de Buenos Aires: the municipally owned central arch is demolished from 9 August 1883 and the work takes eight days. This is stage one of two
stops.campa: For eighty years an arcade has run across the Plaza Mayor, splitting it into two squares, its arches full of shopkeepers. The central arch belongs to the municipality, so the municipality begins there: demolition opens on the ninth of August and takes eight days. The rest of the structure belongs to the Anchorena family and cannot be touched until it has been expropriated. Through that winter the plaza stands half open and half arcaded, with the shopkeepers still trading under the part that is left.
suggested_refs: The Recova de Buenos Aires, built 1802-1804 to a design by Agustin Conde

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the Recova comes down
stops.date_confidence: the main body is demolished 8-14 May 1884 and the plazas are united under one name from 17 May 1884, both attested. The biographies disagree on the year they credit to Buschiazzo: his own article says 1884, Alvear's says 25 May 1883, which matches neither stage. Flagged, not resolved
stops.campa: The expropriation goes through and the main body of the Recova comes down between the eighth and the fourteenth of May. Three days later the two squares are declared a single Plaza de Mayo, and seven hundred workers finish the ground in nine days. His own biography credits him with the demolition and dates it 1884; Alvear's dates it to May of the year before, which matches neither stage of the work. The arcade had stood since 1802. Nothing records what became of the shopkeepers.
stops.quote: Dirigio la demolicion, en 1884, de la Vieja Recova
stops.quote_source: es.wikipedia, Juan Antonio Buschiazzo; an encyclopedia paraphrase, not a period document, and flagged as such
suggested_refs: The union of the Plaza de la Victoria and the Plaza 25 de Mayo, 17 May 1884

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the second Bolsa de Comercio
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: en.wikipedia alone, no month, no independent confirmation of the attribution, and no photograph of the building located
stops.campa: He builds the second headquarters of the stock exchange for a city trading grain, wool and hides in quantities that have outgrown its rooms. The building later passes to the Banco de la Nacion, absorbed rather than kept, and is eventually pulled down. Nothing of it stands. It survives as a line in the list of his works, in a career whose losses are mostly of this kind, not destroyed for any reason worth recording, simply replaced by whatever the block came to be worth.
suggested_refs: The second headquarters of the Bolsa de Comercio de Buenos Aires, demolished

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the Sociedad Central de Arquitectos is founded
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia, Sociedad Central de Arquitectos; en.wikipedia gives only the year
stops.campa: Nine architects meet and constitute the Sociedad Central de Arquitectos, and Argentina has a professional body of architects for the first time. Buschiazzo is one of the nine, alongside Ernesto Bunge, Joaquin Mariano Belgrano and Adolfo Buttner. He will preside over it from 1888 to 1891 and again in 1901 and 1902, and remain its honorary president until he dies. He was trained by apprenticeship in a country with no school, and spends his last thirty years running the institution that ends that arrangement.
suggested_refs: The founding session of the Sociedad Central de Arquitectos, 18 March 1886

stops.name: Palacio de Aguas Corrientes: three hundred thousand pieces
stops.date_confidence: the construction runs 1887-1894, not a single year. Buschiazzo is named as one of the local architects collaborating, not as author. Coordinate re-derived from the block bounded by Cordoba, Riobamba, Viamonte and Ayacucho, since the value in circulation sat several hundred metres southeast of it
stops.campa: Four hundred workers raise a palace to hold water tanks, faced in three hundred thousand enamelled terracotta pieces shipped from Great Britain and numbered for assembly. The Norwegian Olaf Boye and the Swedish engineer Carlos Nystromer lead the work; Buschiazzo is one of the local architects they work with, not the author of it, and the distinction is worth keeping. Buenos Aires has decided that its waterworks should look like a Flemish town hall. It is declared a national monument in 1989.
suggested_refs: Palacio de Aguas Corrientes, Av. Cordoba 1950, national historic monument by decree 325 of 1989

stops.name: Cementerio de la Chacarita: the necropolis he may not have drawn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1887 attribution comes from general repute and the research brief; the cemetery's own article names no architect for this phase at all and never mentions Buschiazzo. Coordinate inherited unchanged from the corpus pin already in use for Chacarita
stops.campa: The yellow fever of 1871 filled the older burial grounds past capacity and forced the city to open an enormous new cemetery on its western edge; the section that starts receiving burials in 1887 is credited to him by long repute. The cemetery's own record names no architect for that phase. Nothing found settles it either way, and the attribution rests on the sort of general agreement that dissolves as soon as anyone asks for a document. By this date he is the man assumed to have drawn any cemetery in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: Cementerio de la Chacarita, the section known as Chacarita la Nueva, opened 1887

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo: the demolitions for the avenue begin
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia, Avenida de Mayo, which dates the start of demolition around the plaza to 25 May 1888 under law 1,583 of 31 October 1884. The Cabildo article dates the same cut to 1889; see the following stop
stops.campa: Law 1,583 authorized the avenue four years ago. On the twenty-fifth of May the demolitions begin around the plaza: the Police House, the Fire Barracks, and three arches off the north side of the Cabildo, which is not being widened around but cut into. The avenue is not a diagonal. It runs straight west along the old Rivadavia and Victoria line, which is exactly why it has to be driven through the middle of built blocks rather than between them, and why every metre of it is somebody's demolished wall.
suggested_refs: Law 1,583 of 31 October 1884, authorizing the opening of the Avenida de Mayo

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the report on paving the city
stops.date_confidence: the year is the publication year of the Anales volume carrying the report; the report's own date is not given in the index line, which is all that could be read
stops.campa: He is president of the architects' society and the city's public works are his desk. With the architect Pablo Biot and the engineers Huergo, Otamendi and White he signs a report to the intendente on how Buenos Aires should be paved: five men on the surfaces a city of mud and stone blocks is about to commit itself to for a century. The report is filed in the annals of the scientific society. Only its heading can be read now. The pages behind the heading did not come up.
stops.quote: Informe sobre pavimentacion de la ciudad, presentado al senor Intendente de la Capital por los senores arquitectos Juan A. Buschiazzo y Pablo Biot e ingenieros Luis A. Huergo, Romulo Otamendi y Guillermo White
stops.quote_source: Table of contents, Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 27 (1889), p. 193, es.wikisource; accents flattened here, article body not retrievable
suggested_refs: Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 27, p. 193

stops.name: Cabildo de Buenos Aires: three arches off the north side
stops.date_confidence: three datings for one event, none preferred here: es.wikipedia Cabildo says 1889 and names the engineer Juan Antonio Buschiazzo; es.wikipedia Avenida de Mayo says the demolitions began 25 May 1888; the Alvear file dates the truncation to 1888-05-25. Coordinate inherited unchanged from the corpus Cabildo pin
stops.campa: As director of public works he orders three arches taken off the northern side of the Cabildo, and the ornamental tower Pedro Benoit added a decade ago comes down with them, its weight judged a risk to the old walls beneath. The town hall of the colony and of the May Revolution loses its symmetry and will not get it back in his lifetime. His own article dates this to 1889; the avenue's article dates the same cut to May 1888. In 1931 the three arches on the southern side will go as well.
suggested_refs: The Cabildo de Buenos Aires before the 1888-89 truncation; Pedro Benoit's tower of 1879

stops.name: Villa Devoto: a plan signed by a Buschiazzo
stops.date_confidence: the founding date is firm; the attribution is not. es.wikipedia, Villa Devoto, credits the plan to the engineers Carlos Buschiazzo and Jose Poggi, and the same article separately credits the 1913 palace here to Juan Antonio Buschiazzo by name, so it is distinguishing the two deliberately
stops.campa: A plan is presented to the municipality for a neighbourhood on the western edge: boulevards and diagonals radiating from a central plaza, laid across land the banker Antonio Devoto has just bought. The record credits it to Jose Poggi and to a Buschiazzo named Carlos, not Juan Antonio, and the same source separately and deliberately credits the palace built here in 1913 to Juan Antonio by his full name. Either two Buschiazzos are drawing plans in Buenos Aires, or one of those lines is wrong, and nothing reachable says which.
suggested_refs: The founding plan of Villa Devoto, presented 13 April 1889, and Plaza Arenales at its centre

stops.name: Bolivar and Avenida de Mayo: the municipal palace
stops.date_confidence: construction runs 1891-1902. The building credited to him here is the municipal Palacio de Gobierno, the city hall. It is not the Casa Rosada, whose own article credits Francesco Tamburini, Henrik Aberg and Carl Kihlberg and never mentions Buschiazzo; earlier notes conflated the two
stops.campa: At Bolivar and the new avenue he builds the municipal palace, an Italian frame under a Frenchified mansard roof, eleven years in the raising. It is the city hall, the seat of the intendencia he has worked for since 1880. It is not the government house of the nation, which stands a short walk east, was unified by Francesco Tamburini with Henrik Aberg and Carl Kihlberg, and carries no mention of him anywhere in its record. Construction runs from 1891 to 1902.
suggested_refs: The municipal Palacio de Gobierno at Bolivar and Avenida de Mayo, 1891-1902

stops.name: Iglesia de la Merced: the facade modified
stops.date_confidence: attested: the remodelling begins in 1894 with Buschiazzo modifying the facade, and the facade is inaugurated 24 April 1900. Earlier notes called this commission undated, which the church's own article contradicts
stops.campa: A colonial church over a century old, and he is asked to change its face. The total remodelling begins in 1894; the new facade is inaugurated on the twenty-fourth of April 1900, with Belgrano carved on it offering his captured flags and his baton to the Virgin. The baroque tower stays where it is. A street away from the exchange and the banks, the oldest thing on the block is given a nineteenth-century front and keeps its eighteenth-century bones.
suggested_refs: Basilica de Nuestra Senora de la Merced, Reconquista 207, facade inaugurated 24 April 1900

stops.name: Avenida de Mayo: the boulevard opened
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is the corpus pin already used for the avenue
stops.campa: The boulevard is inaugurated on the ninth of July, six years after the first wall came down for it. It runs from the plaza west to the ground where Congress will be built, past the Cabildo it amputated and over the site of the Recova it replaced, and it is what makes Buenos Aires legible to Europeans as a European capital. Paris is the stated model. Alvear, who ordered it and fought the property owners for the line of it, has been dead four years and does not see it open.
suggested_refs: The inauguration of the Avenida de Mayo, 9 July 1894

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the anteproyecto for the foundlings
stops.date_confidence: the index line carries no date; the year is the publication year of the Anales volume that holds it. Whether anything was built to this project is not recorded in any source consulted
stops.campa: He works up a preliminary project for a hospital and asylum for abandoned children and describes it in a memoir for the scientific society: the foundlings of a city taking in a hundred thousand immigrants a decade, given a plan and a set of elevations. Whether a brick of it was ever laid does not appear anywhere reachable. The memoir is now a line in a table of contents, page seventy-nine, with the article behind it unretrievable.
stops.quote: Memoria descriptiva del anteproyecto de hospital y asilo de ninos expositos, por Juan A. Buschiazzo
stops.quote_source: Table of contents, Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 37 (1894), p. 79, es.wikisource; accents flattened here, article body not retrievable
suggested_refs: Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 37, p. 79

stops.name: Mercado de San Telmo: iron and glass for Devoto
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by es.wikipedia, Mercado de San Telmo; no month
stops.campa: Antonio Devoto commissions a market and Buschiazzo roofs the middle of a block in iron and glass, the entrance set at Bolivar and Carlos Calvo behind Tuscan columns and rounded arches. Under the glass, meat and vegetables. Outside it, tenements filling with Italians and Spaniards who have to be fed daily and cheaply. Two more wings are added in 1930, thirteen years after his death. The hall still stands and is still a market, its stalls now split between greengrocers and antique dealers.
suggested_refs: Mercado de San Telmo, central body of 1897, entrance at Bolivar and Carlos Calvo

stops.name: Hospital Italiano: the memoir and the building
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the attribution. The hospital's own article gives 1902 for the inauguration of the Almagro headquarters and names no architect in its text, listing Buschiazzo only in its category tags; the research brief gives 1901. His own 1896 memoir on the project in progress is the firmest link
stops.campa: The Italian community of Buenos Aires, by now among the largest outside Italy, builds itself a hospital in Almagro on ground that had belonged to Dalmacio Velez Sarsfield, who wrote the country's civil code. Six years before it opens, Buschiazzo describes the project already under construction in a memoir for the scientific society. The hospital's own history names no architect at all and files him under a category. He came off a boat here at four years old with a mason for a father.
stops.quote: Memoria descriptiva del proyecto de Nuevo Hospital Italiano actualmente en ejecucion, por Juan A. Buschiazzo
stops.quote_source: Table of contents, Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 41 (1896), es.wikisource; article body not retrievable
suggested_refs: Anales de la Sociedad Cientifica Argentina, Tomo 41; Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Peron 4190

stops.name: Parana: the provincial hospitals
stops.date_confidence: none of these provincial commissions carries a date in any source consulted, and the year here is a bare placeholder inside his mature career. The coordinate is the city of Parana, not the hospital site, which is unconfirmed
stops.campa: Upriver in Entre Rios he builds the Hospital San Martin at Parana. There is another San Martin at Mar del Plata, a Vicente Lopez y Planes at General Rodriguez, and a cemetery at Gualeguay, all of them listed among his works and none of them dated in anything that can be read now. Provincial towns want a metropolitan finish on their public institutions and hire the capital's architects to supply it. The buildings went up in places that mostly forgot who drew them.
suggested_refs: Hospital San Martin, Parana; Hospital San Martin, Mar del Plata; Hospital Vicente Lopez y Planes, General Rodriguez; the cemetery of Gualeguay

stops.name: Palermo: the Centennial Exposition commission
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: en.wikipedia alone gives the 1908-1910 span for his part in the commission, with no month and no corroborating source found
stops.campa: He sits on the commission organizing the International Centennial Exposition in Palermo, a hundred years after the May Revolution. Pavilions go up across the park for a single season and most of them come down within months, an architecture built to be photographed and then dismantled. He is sixty-three. For thirty years he has been deciding what Buenos Aires builds and what it pulls down; here both decisions are taken about the same buildings, in advance, by the same committee.
suggested_refs: The Exposicion Internacional del Centenario, Buenos Aires, 1910

stops.name: Hospital Durand: Caballito, the last large commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1909-1912 span by both encyclopedias; no month
stops.campa: On Diaz Velez in Caballito he works three years on the Hospital Durand, one of the last large public commissions of his life. He is in his mid-sixties and has been building hospitals for this city since 1883. The building will itself be demolished and replaced in due course, by the same cycle he once ran from the other end, when the order to pull things down was signed on his desk. Buenos Aires has never kept its public architecture out of tenderness.
suggested_refs: Hospital General de Agudos Dr. Carlos G. Durand, Av. Diaz Velez 5044

stops.name: Villa Devoto: the palace nobody lives in
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by es.wikipedia, Antonio Devoto, which credits Juan Antonio Buschiazzo by name. The coordinate is Plaza Arenales at the centre of the neighbourhood; the palace's own footprint is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Antonio Devoto and his second wife Elina Pombo commission a house of more than ten thousand square metres in the neighbourhood that carries Devoto's name, and Buschiazzo, sixty-eight years old, builds it. Devoto dies in 1916 and Pombo in 1923, and neither of them ever lives in it. What became of the building afterwards, when it came down and on whose order, is documented in nothing that can be reached. The record of it simply stops in 1923, with an empty house of ten thousand metres standing in a neighbourhood named after the man who paid for it.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Devoto, Villa Devoto, 1913; the fate of the building after 1923 is an open gap

stops.name: Gualeguaychu: the Hospital Centenario
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by es.wikipedia; no month, and the coordinate is the town rather than a confirmed hospital site
stops.campa: In a river town in Entre Rios he designs the Hospital Centenario, its name marking the same anniversary that had occupied him on the exposition commission three years before. He is sixty-eight, four years from his death, still producing public buildings for provinces he does not live in and towns he will probably never see finished. It is the last work in his record that carries a date at all. The name outlasts the anniversary it was given for.
suggested_refs: Hospital Centenario, Gualeguaychu, Entre Rios, 1913

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the death of the municipal architect
stops.date_confidence: attested by both encyclopedias; the coordinate is the shared city pin, since no address of death is recorded
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires on the thirteenth of May, seventy-one years old, in the city his family reached by rowboat when he was four. Nearly four decades as a public architect stand behind him: a professional society founded, hospitals in five provinces, markets, churches, two cemeteries, an avenue driven through the colonial centre, and a town hall he took three arches off. The Spanish encyclopedia settles the whole of it into a single phrase.
stops.quote: vinculado su nombre al embellecimiento de Buenos Aires
suggested_refs: Obituary notices in the Buenos Aires press, May 1917 (none located)

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the will and the nephew
stops.date_confidence: the will's provision is attested by es.wikipedia, Mario Buschiazzo, but the document carries no date in any source consulted; placed shortly after the death as a convention. Mario was born 10 December 1902, so any account making him a working historian in 1917 is impossible
stops.campa: His will provides for the education of his nephew Mario, who is fourteen and at school. The boy will become the leading architectural historian in the country, and in 1940 will begin the first scientific restoration of a national historical monument ever attempted here. The monument is the Cabildo. The uncle's money pays for the training of the man who will spend twenty years repairing the building the uncle cut, and the family record of it consists of a single word: tio.
suggested_refs: The testament of Juan Antonio Buschiazzo, 1917, provision for Mario Buschiazzo (1902-1970)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: in through his own gate
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Recoleta is attested; the exact day is not recorded, and the day after the death is taken as the convention. No plot number, no description of the vault, and no photograph of it were located
stops.campa: He is carried up the slope and in through four Doric columns he set there thirty-six years earlier, past the wall he built and along the paved avenues he drew, to lie among the families whose tombs came after his gate. No plot number is recorded. No description of the vault survives, and no photograph of it has been found. Nothing on record marks that the architect of the entrance is inside it. The cemetery has gone on filling ever since, marble folded on marble.
suggested_refs: The grave of Juan Antonio Buschiazzo, Cementerio de la Recoleta, plot unrecorded

stops.name: Cabildo de Buenos Aires: the nephew's restoration
stops.date_confidence: attested: 11 October 1940 is the inauguration of the first phase, not the completion. The work runs to 1960. Coordinate inherited unchanged from the corpus Cabildo pin
stops.campa: Fifty-one years after the arches came off, his nephew begins putting the Cabildo back: the upper floor rebuilt, the Sala Capitular restored, the tower recast in reinforced concrete and deliberately made shorter than the colonial one, because at full colonial height it would look wrong on what is left of the building. Concrete where there was masonry, so that the repair can always be told from the thing repaired. The work is inaugurated in phases and runs to 1960.
suggested_refs: Mario Buschiazzo's restoration of the Cabildo, 1940-1960, the first scientific restoration of a national historical monument in Argentina

stops.name: Cabildo de Buenos Aires: the digging underneath
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1991-1992 excavation seasons; no month
stops.campa: The archaeologist Daniel Schavelzon digs beneath the Cabildo for two seasons and comes up with the eighteenth-century floors, the wells, the buried rubbish of a building standing here since before the viceroyalty. What he writes of the structure over his head is that it has been cut back twice by street widening. The first of those cuts was ordered from Buschiazzo's desk to open the Avenida de Mayo; the second went through in 1931, over a newspaper campaign. The building is now narrower than any century that drew it intended.
suggested_refs: Daniel Schavelzon's excavations beneath the Cabildo de Buenos Aires, 1991-1992
